title: Part 1, Chapter 3
paragraphs: In which the droll way Don Quixote had himself dubbed a knight is described

Worn down by this thought, he hurried through his cheap inn supper, called for the innkeeper, shut himself with him in the stable, and fell on his knees in front of him, saying, "Valiant knight, I will not rise from this spot until your courtesy grants me a favour I am about to ask — a favour that will redound to your praise and the benefit of all humanity." The innkeeper, seeing his guest at his feet and hearing this kind of talk, stood staring, baffled, not sure what to do or say, and kept urging him to get up — but he wouldn't, until the innkeeper agreed to grant the favour. "I expected no less, my lord, of your high magnanimity," replied Don Quixote, "and I have to tell you that the favour I asked, and your generosity has granted, is that tomorrow morning you will dub me a knight, and that tonight I will watch my armour in the chapel of this castle of yours; so that tomorrow, as I have said, what I so much desire will be accomplished, enabling me to roam lawfully throughout all four quarters of the world in search of adventures on behalf of those in distress, as is the duty of chivalry and of knights-errant such as myself, whose ambition is bent on deeds of that kind."

The innkeeper, who, as has been mentioned, was something of a joker, and had already suspected his guest of being out of his wits, was now sure of it on hearing this. To make the evening more amusing, he decided to play along. So he told Don Quixote that he was quite right to pursue this object, and that such a motive was natural and becoming in cavaliers as distinguished as he plainly was; and that he himself, in his younger days, had followed the same honourable calling, ranging in quest of adventures in various parts of the country — the Curing-grounds of Málaga, the Isles of Riarán, the Compass of Seville, the Little Market of Segovia, the Olivera of Valencia, the Rondilla of Granada, the Strand of Sanlúcar, the Colt of Córdoba, the Taverns of Toledo, and various other neighbourhoods, where he had tested the lightness of his feet and the nimbleness of his fingers — doing many wrongs, cheating many widows, ruining a fair number of maidens, swindling minors, and in short bringing himself to the attention of nearly every tribunal and court of justice in Spain — until at last he had retired to this castle of his, where he was living on his own income and other people's, and where he received all knights-errant of whatever rank or condition, out of the great love he bore them, and so that they might share their funds with him in return for his hospitality. He further told him that this castle of his had no chapel where he could keep vigil over his armour, because it had been pulled down for rebuilding; but that in an emergency it could be kept anywhere, and he could keep watch tonight in a courtyard, and in the morning, God willing, the proper ceremonies would be performed and he would be dubbed a knight — and so thoroughly dubbed that no one in the world would be more so. He asked if he had any money on him, to which Don Quixote replied that he did not have a penny, since in the histories of knights-errant he had never read of any of them carrying any. The innkeeper told him he was mistaken: although it was not mentioned in the histories — because in the authors' opinion there was no need to mention something as obvious and necessary as money and clean shirts — it was not therefore to be supposed they did without them, and he could take it as certain and established that all knights-errant (about whom there were so many lengthy and trustworthy books) carried well-stocked purses for emergencies, and also carried shirts and a small box of ointment to treat the wounds they received. For on those plains and in those deserts where they fought and came out wounded, there was not always someone to bandage them up, unless they had as a friend some wise enchanter who would send them help on the spot, fetching through the air on a cloud some damsel or dwarf with a flask of water of such power that a single drop would cure all their hurts on the instant and leave them as sound as if nothing had happened. But in case that didn't happen, the knights of old took care to see their squires were provided with money and other necessities, such as lint and ointments for healing; and when knights had no squires (which was rare), they themselves carried everything in cunning saddle-bags so small they hardly showed on the horse's croup, as if they were something else of more importance — because, except for some such reason, carrying saddle-bags was not very well thought of among knights-errant. He therefore advised him (and, as his godson-to-be, he might even command him) never from that day forward to travel without money and the usual necessities, and he would find the benefit of them when he least expected it.

Don Quixote promised to follow this advice to the letter, and it was arranged at once that he should keep vigil over his armour in a large yard at one side of the inn. So, gathering it all together, Don Quixote laid it on a trough that stood beside a well, braced his shield on his arm, took up his lance, and with a stately air began to march up and down in front of the trough. As he began his patrol, night began to fall.

The innkeeper told everyone at the inn about his guest's craze, the watching of the armour, and the dubbing ceremony he was planning. Astonished at so strange a form of madness, they came out to see from a distance, and watched as he sometimes paced up and down with composure, sometimes leaned on his lance and stared at his armour without taking his eyes off it for the longest time. Night closed in with a moonlight so bright it might have rivalled the sun that loaned it, so that everything the new knight did was clearly seen by everyone.

Meanwhile, one of the carriers at the inn took it into his head to water his team, and to do so it was necessary to move Don Quixote's armour off the trough. Don Quixote, seeing him approach, called out in a loud voice, "O you, whoever you are, rash knight who comes to lay hands on the armour of the most valiant knight-errant that ever girt on a sword — beware what you do; do not touch it, unless you wish to pay for your rashness with your life." The carrier paid no attention to these words (he would have been better off if he had), but grabbed the armour by the straps and flung it some distance away. Seeing this, Don Quixote raised his eyes to heaven, fixed his thoughts (apparently) on his lady Dulcinea, and exclaimed, "Help me, my lady, in this first encounter offered to this breast you hold in thrall; let your favour and protection not fail me in this first peril." With these and other words to the same effect, he dropped his shield, lifted his lance with both hands, and brought it down on the carrier's head with such force that he laid him out on the ground; one more such blow would have spared the surgeon a job. Done with that, he picked up his armour and returned to his patrol with the same serenity as before.

Shortly after, another carrier, not knowing what had happened (the first still lay senseless), came with the same intention of watering his mules, and was about to move the armour off the trough when Don Quixote — without a word or a call for help — once again dropped his shield, lifted his lance, and without quite cracking the second carrier's head open made three or four pieces of it, splitting it in four places. At the noise the whole inn came running, the innkeeper with them. Seeing this, Don Quixote braced his shield on his arm, put his hand on his sword, and exclaimed, "O Lady of Beauty, strength and support of my fainting heart, it is time to turn the eyes of your greatness upon this your captive knight on the brink of so mighty an adventure." That inspired him enough that he would not have flinched if all the carriers in the world had attacked him. The companions of the wounded, seeing the state they were in, began at a distance to rain stones down on Don Quixote, who shielded himself as best he could, not daring to leave the trough and abandon his armour. The innkeeper shouted at them to leave him alone, saying he had already told them the man was mad, and as a madman he would not be held to account even if he killed every one of them. Don Quixote shouted louder, calling them knaves and traitors, and calling the lord of the castle — for letting knights-errant be treated in this way — a villain and a base-born knight, whom, had he himself been knighted, he would call to account for his treachery. "But of you," he cried, "base and vile rabble, I take no notice. Throw, strike, come on — do whatever you can against me; you'll see the reward of your folly and insolence." He said this with such force and boldness that he filled his attackers with real fear, and as much for that reason as because of the innkeeper's pleas, they stopped stoning him. He allowed them to carry off the wounded, and with the same calm and composure as before resumed the watch over his armour.

But these antics of his guest did not at all please the innkeeper, who decided to cut the business short and bestow on him at once the wretched order of knighthood before any further mishap could occur. So, going up to him, he apologised for the rudeness which, without his knowledge, had been shown to him by those low people — who, he said, had been well punished for their audacity. As he had already told him, there was no chapel in the castle, but it wasn't needed for what remained to be done; as he understood the ceremony, the whole point of being dubbed a knight lay in the accolade and in the slap on the shoulder, and that could be administered in the middle of a field. He had already done all that was needed by way of watching the armour, since the requirement was satisfied by a two-hour watch, and he had been at it more than four. Don Quixote believed everything and said he stood there ready to obey, asking only that the business be ended as quickly as possible — for, if he were attacked again and felt himself dubbed a knight, he didn't think he would leave a soul alive in the castle, except for those he might spare out of respect at the innkeeper's request.

So warned, and so threatened, the castellan brought out a book in which he used to enter the straw and barley he issued to the carriers, and with a boy carrying a candle stub and the two damsels already mentioned, he came back to where Don Quixote stood and ordered him to kneel. Then, reading from his account-book as if he were reciting a prayer, halfway through he raised his hand and gave him a hearty blow on the neck, and after that, with the man's own sword, a smart slap on the shoulder — muttering between his teeth the whole time as though he were at prayer. When this was done, he directed one of the ladies to gird on his sword, which she did with great self-possession and gravity, though it took some doing to keep herself from bursting out laughing at each stage of the ceremony; what they had already seen of the novice knight's prowess kept the laughter in check. As she girded on the sword the good woman said, "May God make your worship a fortunate knight and give you success in battle." Don Quixote asked her name, so that he might know from then on to whom he was indebted for the favour received, since he meant to give her some share of whatever honour he won by the might of his arm. She answered, very humbly, that her name was La Tolosa, and that she was the daughter of a cobbler in Toledo who lived in the stalls of Sanchobienaya, and that wherever she was she would serve and respect him as her lord. Don Quixote replied that she would do him a favour if from now on she took the "Doña" and called herself Doña Tolosa. She promised she would. Then the other buckled on his spur, and with her he had practically the same conversation as with the lady of the sword. He asked her name, and she said it was La Molinera, that she was the daughter of a respectable miller of Antequera; and of her likewise Don Quixote asked that she take the "Doña" and call herself Doña Molinera, with offers of further service and favours.

Having brought these never-before-seen ceremonies to a hasty close, Don Quixote was on tenterhooks until he saw himself in the saddle and on his way out in search of adventures. He saddled Rocinante at once, mounted, and embracing his host, he thanked him for knighting him in language so extravagant that it is impossible to convey it, let alone report it. The innkeeper, to get him out of the inn, replied with no less rhetoric, if in fewer words, and without making him pay the bill let him ride off with a God-speed.
